content.intro: This lesson covers Continuous Integration for Rust Projects. It sits in Module 27, Professional Rust Tooling and Team Workflows, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: Continuous Integration for Rust Projects matters when you work with repeatable quality checks and feedback. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Rust tooling makes the build, dependency graph, formatting, linting, and test steps repeatable. Use the project’s declared toolchain and Cargo metadata rather than relying on undocumented local state.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For Continuous Integration for Rust Projects, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. A professional workflow automates formatting, linting, tests, dependency review, and reproducible builds. Review edition migrations and public API changes before merging.

cargo fmt --check
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo test --all-targets

content_blocks.reset_steps: Return the sample to its original form, run the documented command again, and compare the result. If a dependency, target, runtime, database, or hardware device is required, configure that separately before treating the result as verified.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not assume Continuous Integration for Rust Projects guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.

content_blocks.title: Toolchain and execution boundary
content_blocks.text: Course examples are static reference snippets, not executed inside CodeLeaf. Most standard-library examples can be tried in a Rust 2024 Cargo project; specialized networking, database, async, procedural-macro, embedded, and WebAssembly scenarios require the toolchain and dependencies described in their lessons.
